name: Roanoke
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Roanoke, VA | Genstone
metaDescription: Roanoke investor rehabs for Old Southwest Victorians, Raleigh Court bungalows and Southeast railroad houses: hillside lots, oil tanks and local permits.
intro:
Roanoke grew almost overnight in the 1880s when two railroads met in a small depot town called Big Lick, and the city still carries the houses that boom produced. Victorian mansions in Old Southwest, modest frame railroad worker homes in Belmont and Southeast, streetcar-era bungalows in Raleigh Court and Grandin Village, and postwar brick along Williamson Road all sit within a valley ringed by mountains. Hills, creeks and older heating systems shape renovation here in ways that eastern Virginia investors do not always expect.

Genstone Construction renovates Roanoke properties for investors, lenders and servicers who want those conditions priced before they buy. Every job begins with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review and a line-item scope with a draw schedule. A designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors through permits, design review where it applies, and final inspection. You pay nothing up front, and draws follow completed work.
housingStock:
The railroad set Roanoke's housing pattern. When the Norfolk and Western made the city its headquarters, workers needed housing near the shops and yards, and neighborhoods like Belmont, Fallon Park, Southeast and the northwest blocks filled with narrow two-story frame houses, small cottages and some brick rows from the 1890s into the 1920s. Managers and merchants built larger homes in Old Southwest, where Queen Anne, Second Empire, Colonial Revival and Foursquare houses with deep porches line streets climbing from the downtown edge. Gainsboro, the historic center of the city's Black community, holds homes and institutions from the same period.

Streetcar lines then pushed development west and south. Raleigh Court, Grandin Village, Wasena and South Roanoke grew from the 1910s through the early 1940s with Craftsman bungalows, Tudor Revival cottages, Dutch Colonials and brick Colonial Revival homes. After the Second World War, Williamson Road, Villa Heights, Garden City and much of the northeast filled with brick ranches, Cape Cods and split-levels.

Topography changes the building details. Roanoke is hilly, so houses often sit on sloped lots with partial basements, walkout lower levels, stone or block foundations and retaining walls. Older homes commonly have rubble-stone or brick foundations that leak and need parging, drainage or repointing. Many prewar houses were heated by coal and later converted to oil, leaving abandoned oil tanks, either in basements or buried in yards, plus radiators and old boilers. Expect knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, cast-iron drains and lead paint in anything prewar, and asbestos in pipe insulation, flooring and siding from the middle of the century.

For investors, Roanoke houses often deliver solid bones and good square footage at purchase prices that leave room for real renovation, but foundations, heating systems and drainage on slopes deserve the most attention in the budget.

commonIssues.title: Old oil tanks and heating conversions
commonIssues.body: Many older Roanoke homes heated with coal, then oil, before switching to gas or heat pumps. The leftover oil tank, whether in the basement or buried in the yard, can complicate a sale, an insurance policy or a lender's review. Buried tanks may need locating, testing and proper abandonment or removal. We look for fill pipes, vent pipes and basement tanks during the pre-offer review, because tank work is easier to price before you close than after a buyer's inspector finds it.

commonIssues.title: Stone foundations on sloped lots
commonIssues.body: Roanoke's hills put many older houses on rubble-stone or brick foundations with one side buried against a slope. Water from uphill finds its way through mortar joints, leaving damp basements, efflorescence and sometimes bowing walls. Repairs range from regrading and gutters to interior drainage, repointing, parging or structural reinforcement. We assess the slope, the drainage path and the wall condition together, since fixing only the visible symptom rarely keeps a Roanoke basement dry.

commonIssues.title: Creek and river flooding
commonIssues.body: The Roanoke River and creeks such as Peters Creek, Tinker Creek and Lick Run have a long flood history, including the major flood of 1985 that reshaped the city's flood planning. Homes near those waterways may sit in mapped flood zones or simply take water in heavy storms. We check flood maps and local history before scoping, since renovation limits and insurance costs apply in mapped zones.

commonIssues.title: Railroad-era framing and additions
commonIssues.body: Southeast and Belmont worker houses were built quickly and economically, and many have had rear additions, enclosed porches and kitchen bump-outs added over the decades with varied quality. Undersized framing, additions settling away from the main house, and porch roofs tied poorly into the original structure are common. We inspect where old and new framing meet, because those joints are where leaks, rot and sagging tend to concentrate.

commonIssues.title: Asbestos in mid-century materials
commonIssues.body: Homes from the 1940s through the 1970s along Williamson Road and in the northeast neighborhoods frequently contain asbestos in pipe insulation, nine-inch floor tiles, mastic, textured ceilings and cement siding. Older boilers in prewar houses often have asbestos insulation as well. Disturbing those materials during renovation requires testing and proper abatement. We flag suspect materials before demolition, so abatement is in the budget and the schedule instead of stopping work midway.

investorMarket:
Roanoke's investor market is steadier and less speculative than Virginia's larger metros. Purchase prices are moderate, employment is anchored by Carilion Clinic, the Virginia Tech Carilion medical school, manufacturing and regional services, and the outdoor economy has drawn new residents to the valley.

Resale flips perform best in Raleigh Court, Grandin Village, South Roanoke and Wasena, where buyers want renovated bungalows and Colonial Revival homes near the Grandin Village shops, the greenway and the hospital. Old Southwest offers large Victorians with strong character, but renovations there are bigger projects, and exterior work is subject to design review.

Rental and BRRRR strategies tend to work in Belmont, Fallon Park, Melrose-Rugby, Williamson Road and Villa Heights, where lower purchase prices and sturdy postwar or early-twentieth-century houses support rents from hospital staff, service workers and families. Some of those neighborhoods are in the middle of revitalization, so buying on the right block matters.

Small multifamily is concentrated in Old Southwest and nearby neighborhoods, where large homes were converted to apartments decades ago. Those buildings need careful review of unit counts, fire separation and heating systems.

Across all of them, foundation and drainage condition drive renovation cost more than finishes, and the pre-offer review should focus there first.
permits:
Inside the city limits, building permits are issued by the City of Roanoke's Planning, Building and Development department, which enforces the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. Electrical, plumbing, mechanical, structural, roofing and window replacement work generally requires permits, with inspections at rough-in and final stages. Roanoke County, Salem and Vinton each handle their own permits, so properties just over the city line follow different offices.

Roanoke has historic overlay districts reviewed by the city's Architectural Review Board. The H-2 Neighborhood Preservation district covers much of Old Southwest, and exterior changes visible from the street there, such as windows, doors, porches, siding and roofing, generally need a Certificate of Appropriateness.

In mapped flood zones along the Roanoke River and its creeks, floodplain rules apply, including FEMA's substantial improvement standard for larger renovations. Oil tank removal or abandonment may involve state environmental requirements. Contractors must hold a Virginia Board for Contractors license at the right class, and Genstone handles permit applications, inspections and lien waivers on every project.
climate:
Roanoke has four real seasons. Summers are warm and humid, but the valley's higher ground gives slightly milder nights than eastern Virginia. Winters are colder, with regular freezes, periodic snow and occasional ice, and the freeze-thaw cycle works on masonry, retaining walls, concrete steps and driveways on sloped lots.

For rehab scheduling, exterior masonry and concrete work are easiest from mid-spring through early fall, when mortar and concrete cure properly. Heating systems matter more here than in coastal Virginia, so furnace, boiler or heat pump work should be completed before cold weather sets in on a winter renovation. Vacant houses need proper winterization, especially those with old boilers and radiators that can freeze and split.

Heavy summer storms and remnants of tropical systems can bring intense rainfall that overwhelms creeks and pushes water toward basements on hillside lots. Grading and gutter work belongs early in the scope.

faqs.q: Do you deal with old oil tanks on Roanoke properties?
faqs.a: Yes. Many prewar Roanoke homes still have oil tanks in basements or buried in yards from earlier heating systems. During the pre-offer review, we look for fill and vent pipes and basement tanks. If a tank is found, the scope includes the appropriate steps, such as testing, removal or proper abandonment, so it does not become a problem at sale, refinance or insurance renewal. Pricing that before closing gives you something concrete to negotiate with.

faqs.q: Is Old Southwest a good area for investor renovations?
faqs.a: It can be, with the right expectations. Old Southwest has large Victorian homes with strong character and good proximity to downtown and the hospital, but renovations there are usually bigger projects involving foundations, heating, wiring and exterior restoration. Exterior changes visible from the street need Architectural Review Board approval. Investors who plan for that work and the review timeline can do well with flips, rentals or small multifamily conversions.

faqs.q: How do hillside lots affect Roanoke renovation costs?
faqs.a: Sloped lots push water toward foundations and basements, especially on older homes with stone or brick foundations. Fixing that may require regrading, gutters, interior drainage, repointing or structural reinforcement. Steep driveways and limited access can also make deliveries, dumpsters and equipment harder to stage. We factor site access and drainage into the estimate, so the budget reflects the real cost of working on Roanoke's hills.

faqs.q: Do you work in Salem, Vinton and Roanoke County too?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed contractors throughout the Roanoke Valley, including Salem, Vinton and unincorporated Roanoke County areas like Cave Spring and Hollins. Each jurisdiction has its own permit office and timelines. Housing there tends to be newer, especially in Roanoke County subdivisions, so scopes generally shift from foundation and heating work toward kitchens, baths and system updates. Salem and Vinton also keep some older downtown-area housing that looks much like the city's.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Roanoke, VA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Roanoke flip renovations for Raleigh Court and Grandin bungalows, South Roanoke homes and Old Southwest Victorians, scoped for basements, oil tanks and comps.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Roanoke
fix-flip.intro:
A Roanoke flip often starts with a bungalow on a hillside lot in Raleigh Court or Wasena: good proportions, original woodwork, a dated kitchen and a basement that smells damp after rain. Buyers here appreciate character, and the neighborhoods near Grandin Village, South Roanoke and the greenway reward careful renovation. The risk is below grade, in stone foundations, drainage on sloped lots and forgotten oil tanks.

Genstone Construction scopes Roanoke flips with those risks in view. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks the foundation, basement drainage, heating system and any tank evidence, then refines your after-repair value against renovated sales nearby. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local contractors, and draws are paid as milestones are completed. That way your offer reflects the whole house, not just the parts that photograph well.

sections.h2: What Roanoke buyers pay for in renovated bungalows
sections.body:
Buyers in Raleigh Court, Grandin Village and Wasena tend to be hospital staff, young professionals and families who want walkable neighborhoods with original character. They respond to refinished oak or heart pine floors, restored built-ins and original doors and trim, paired with modern kitchens and baths that fit the house's era rather than mimicking new construction.

A second full bathroom often makes a significant difference in older Roanoke bungalows, which commonly had just one. Finishing an attic with proper headroom and egress, or turning a dry walkout basement into usable space, can also add value where the comps support it.

In South Roanoke, buyers expect a more complete renovation, with higher-end kitchens, updated primary suites and outdoor living space. In Old Southwest, Victorian character is the main draw, and buyers expect restoration of porches, windows and interior detail.

We write scopes with multiple finish levels where the comparables support it, so you can compare the cost of each tier against recent sales on similar streets before deciding how far to go.

sections.h2: Basements, drainage and oil tanks on Roanoke flips
sections.body:
The surprises that hurt Roanoke flip budgets are usually underground. Stone and brick foundations on sloped lots let water through mortar joints, leaving damp basements, efflorescence and sometimes bowing walls. Gutters dumping water at the foundation and grading that slopes toward the house make it worse.

We evaluate drainage from the uphill side of the lot down. Fixes may include regrading, extended downspouts, French drains, interior drainage, repointing or parging, and structural reinforcement for bowing walls. Correcting water before finishing a basement is essential, because buyer inspectors in Roanoke routinely check for moisture and efflorescence.

Old oil tanks are the other common surprise. Fill pipes in the yard, vent pipes on the side of the house or an abandoned tank in the basement can all show up on a buyer's inspection. We look for those signs during the pre-offer review, so tank testing, removal or abandonment can be priced into your offer instead of becoming a renegotiation during the buyer's due diligence period.

sections.h2: Design review and seasons in a Roanoke flip schedule
sections.body:
Two factors affect carrying time on a Roanoke flip: design review and weather. In the Old Southwest H-2 district, exterior changes like windows, porches and siding require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Architectural Review Board. We prepare those applications early and sequence interior work in parallel, so the house keeps moving.

Weather plays a bigger role in Roanoke than in coastal Virginia. Masonry repointing, foundation parging and concrete work are best done from mid-spring through early fall, when temperatures allow proper curing. Winter flips should prioritize interior work and get heating systems running early. Steep driveways and narrow streets can complicate deliveries and dumpster placement during snow or ice.

Your field manager handles permits with the city's Planning, Building and Development department, schedules inspections and posts progress photos so you can follow the job remotely. Draws follow completed milestones, final payment follows your approval, and the house goes to market with permits closed and documentation ready for the buyer's agent and inspector.

faqs.q: Which Roanoke neighborhoods work best for flips?
faqs.a: Raleigh Court, Grandin Village, Wasena and South Roanoke tend to produce the strongest resale results, because buyers value their walkability, character and proximity to the hospital and greenway. Old Southwest can work well for larger Victorian projects with design review. The right choice depends on purchase price, foundation condition and comparable sales on your specific street, which we review in the pre-offer analysis.

faqs.q: Should I finish the basement on a Roanoke flip?
faqs.a: Only if it is dry or can be made dry reliably. Many Roanoke basements have stone or brick foundations that leak on sloped lots. If drainage can be corrected with grading, gutters, interior drainage and repointing, a finished walkout basement can add value. If water issues persist, finishing the space creates risk at inspection and after the sale, so we price the drainage work first.

faqs.q: What happens if a buyer's inspector finds an oil tank?
faqs.a: It usually leads to a renegotiation or delay, which is why we look for tank evidence before you buy. If we find fill or vent pipes or a basement tank, we include testing and removal or abandonment in the scope. Having that work completed and documented before listing removes a common source of friction during the buyer's due diligence period.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Roanoke, VA | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Roanoke BRRRR rehabs in Belmont, Melrose-Rugby, Williamson Road and Wasena: renovate to the refinance appraisal with heating, basement and durable fixes.
brrrr.intro:
Roanoke's moderate purchase prices make the BRRRR math easier to pencil than in Richmond or Hampton Roads, but the city's older homes require discipline. A Belmont frame house or a Williamson Road ranch can cycle well through a refinance, but only if the rehab addresses heating, foundations and drainage while keeping finishes appropriate for rental use. Overbuilding in a moderate-value neighborhood is the most common way to strand cash in a Roanoke BRRRR.

Genstone Construction scopes BRRRR projects in Roanoke to reach a solid refinance appraisal with durable, rental-grade work. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and tests the after-repair value against likely comparables. Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit, which you can discuss with them directly when planning the refinance.

sections.h2: Reaching the refinance appraisal in Roanoke
sections.body:
Appraisals in Roanoke vary considerably between neighborhoods and even between blocks. A renovated house in Wasena may draw from strong comparables near Grandin Village, while a similar house in Belmont or Melrose-Rugby may rely on a thinner set of renovated sales.

We review likely comparables before writing the scope. Items that tend to move a Roanoke appraisal include adding a bathroom to a one-bath house, updating the kitchen, installing central air, replacing an outdated heating system, fixing the roof and correcting foundation issues. Finished basement space counts less than above-grade space, so it should only be added if it is dry and the comps support it.

Documentation supports the appraisal. We provide permits, inspection sign-offs and photos of structural work, drainage corrections, heating replacements and any oil tank removal. Those records help appraisers and lenders understand what was improved and why the house is worth the value you need. Missing paperwork on hidden work leaves value on the table at refinance.

sections.h2: Heating and foundation choices for Roanoke rentals
sections.body:
Heating matters in Roanoke because winters are colder than eastern Virginia. Older homes may have oil boilers, radiators, aging furnaces or a mix of systems. For a rental, the choice is between keeping a working hydronic system, converting to gas where service is available, or installing heat pumps with ductwork or ductless units.

We evaluate the existing system, the house layout and the operating cost for the tenant. A heat pump with properly sized ducts can provide both heating and cooling, which tenants value. In houses without ductwork, ductless mini-splits avoid tearing into plaster walls. Old oil tanks are removed or properly abandoned to avoid issues at refinance.

Foundation and drainage work protects the investment over a long hold. Stone foundations get repointed or parged, gutters and grading carry water away, and basements get vapor control where needed. Those items cost more at renovation but prevent water damage, mold complaints and structural problems that would otherwise erode cash flow during the rental period.

sections.h2: Choosing Roanoke BRRRR properties by neighborhood
sections.body:
Not every Roanoke neighborhood performs the same in a BRRRR cycle. Williamson Road, Villa Heights and Garden City offer postwar brick ranches and Cape Cods that are simpler to renovate, with predictable layouts and fewer structural surprises. Rents there are moderate, but renovation costs are also more contained.

Belmont, Fallon Park and Southeast offer older frame homes at lower purchase prices. These houses can produce strong returns but carry more risk in foundations, framing additions and heating systems. Revitalization in parts of Southeast has improved some blocks faster than others, so careful block-by-block selection matters.

Wasena and parts of Raleigh Court offer higher rents and stronger appraisals but at higher purchase prices, which can compress the spread you need for a successful refinance. We help you compare those tradeoffs during the pre-offer review. If the numbers do not support a refinance at the asking price, we will say so before you buy rather than after the appraisal comes back short.

faqs.q: Should I convert an old oil boiler in a Roanoke rental?
faqs.a: It depends on the system's condition and fuel availability. A working hydronic system can provide comfortable heat, but oil costs and maintenance may concern tenants and lenders. Converting to gas or installing heat pumps adds cooling and usually simplifies operation. We price each option so you can compare upfront cost against long-term operating and maintenance costs for the hold. If the tank stays in service, expect the appraiser and DSCR lender to ask about it.

faqs.q: Which Roanoke neighborhoods suit BRRRR?
faqs.a: Williamson Road, Villa Heights and Garden City offer simpler postwar homes with predictable renovation costs. Belmont, Fallon Park and Southeast offer older homes at lower prices with more risk and upside. Wasena and Raleigh Court produce stronger appraisals at higher purchase prices. The best fit depends on your budget, risk tolerance and the comparable sales on the specific block. Revitalizing streets in Southeast can change quickly, so recent sales matter more than older ones there.

faqs.q: Does a finished basement help a Roanoke refinance appraisal?
faqs.a: It helps less than above-grade space, and only if the basement is reliably dry. Appraisers generally value below-grade space at a lower rate. In Roanoke, many basements need drainage work before finishing makes sense. We recommend correcting water issues first and finishing only where comparables show buyers and appraisers value the space. A walkout lower level on a Wasena hillside, with windows and a door at grade, is the most likely to earn credit.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Roanoke, VA | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovations in Roanoke: portfolio specs adapted to stone basements, older heating, hillside drainage and lead-safe work in prewar homes.
rental-renovation.intro:
Roanoke single-family rentals are often older than portfolio operators expect. A typical holding might include a 1920s frame house in Belmont, a bungalow in Wasena, and a 1950s brick ranch off Williamson Road. Each leases well to hospital employees, service workers and families, but each brings different heating, foundation and drainage issues, and colder winters make heating reliability a bigger part of tenant satisfaction than it is in the eastern part of the state.

Genstone Construction renovates single-family rentals in Roanoke for landlords, funds and portfolio operators. We build scopes from your finish standard, add the building-specific items each house needs, and coordinate licensed local trades through permits and inspections. Genstone Field Services handles turns, make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance, so the same family of companies can support the property after renovation.

sections.h2: Adapting a portfolio standard to Roanoke's older homes
sections.body:
A consistent finish package of flooring, paint, fixtures, cabinets and appliances keeps maintenance simple across a Roanoke portfolio. What varies is the work each house needs beneath those finishes.

Prewar frame houses in Belmont and Southeast often need foundation repointing or drainage work, electrical upgrades to replace knob-and-tube, heating system replacement and lead-safe work on windows and trim. Bungalows in Wasena and Raleigh Court may need basement moisture control and plumbing updates. Postwar ranches along Williamson Road often need asbestos abatement in flooring or pipe insulation, HVAC replacement and window upgrades.

We list those building-specific items separately from your standard finish package. That lets you compare properties fairly, understand why one house costs more than another, and plan future acquisitions with better information about which neighborhoods and house types carry more hidden costs. Over time, a portfolio renovated to one standard also allows your maintenance team to stock fewer parts and respond to calls faster.

sections.h2: Heating, basements and tenant comfort in Roanoke
sections.body:
Tenant calls in Roanoke rentals often trace back to cold weather and water. Old boilers that fail in January, drafty windows and uninsulated attics generate heating complaints. Damp basements, musty odors and occasional water intrusion after heavy rain produce another set of calls.

We address those at renovation. Heating systems are evaluated and replaced or converted as needed, with heat pumps often providing both heat and air conditioning. Attics get insulation and air sealing, and windows are replaced or repaired where they are drafty or failing.

Basements get attention from the outside in. Gutters and downspouts carry water away from the foundation, grading slopes away from the house, and stone or brick foundations are repointed or parged. Where needed, interior drainage and dehumidification keep basements dry. Those investments cost little compared with years of repair calls, tenant turnover and potential water damage, and they make Roanoke rentals more comfortable through the city's colder winters.

sections.h2: Lead-safe work, oil tanks and Roanoke compliance
sections.body:
Most Roanoke rental stock was built before 1978, so lead-based paint is expected on windows, doors, trim and exteriors. Work that disturbs painted surfaces in pre-1978 rentals falls under the EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, which requires certified renovators, containment and cleaning verification. We include those practices in every older-house scope and provide documentation for your records.

Old oil tanks are another compliance issue. A tank left in the basement or buried in the yard can complicate insurance, refinancing or a future sale. We look for evidence during the pre-offer review and include removal or proper abandonment in the scope.

Permits for electrical, plumbing, mechanical and structural work go through the city's Planning, Building and Development department, and we close them before returning the property. Genstone Field Services handles turns with the original scope and finishes on file, so matching materials can be ordered quickly and the house can be leased again with minimal downtime.

faqs.q: What heating system works best for Roanoke rentals?
faqs.a: Heat pumps are often a good fit because they provide heating and cooling with one system. In older homes without ductwork, ductless mini-splits avoid opening plaster walls. Where a hydronic system works well, keeping it may make sense, but oil heat often concerns tenants and lenders. We evaluate each house and price the options so you can compare cost and comfort.

faqs.q: How do you handle damp basements in Roanoke rentals?
faqs.a: We start with water management outside the house, including gutters, downspout extensions and grading. Stone or brick foundations are repointed or parged as needed. Where water still enters, interior drainage and dehumidification keep the basement dry. Addressing those issues at renovation reduces mold complaints and protects the structure over a long hold. On steep lots in South Roanoke or Wasena, we start on the uphill side, since that is usually where the water comes from.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a mixed Roanoke portfolio to one standard?
faqs.a: Yes. We apply your finish standard across properties and list building-specific work, like foundation repairs, heating replacements or asbestos abatement, separately. That keeps maintenance consistent and helps you compare properties, while still addressing the different needs of prewar frame homes, bungalows and postwar ranches. A Belmont house and a Garden City ranch can share flooring, paint and fixtures even though the work underneath them is very different.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation in Roanoke, VA | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Renovating Roanoke duplexes and converted Victorians in Old Southwest, Gainsboro and Grandin: unit separation, boilers, egress and design review.
multifamily-renovation.intro:
Small multifamily in Roanoke is mostly found inside old houses. Large Victorians in Old Southwest were divided into apartments during the mid-twentieth century, bungalows near Grandin and Wasena were split into up-and-down duplexes, and some neighborhoods near downtown have small brick walk-ups from the early 1900s. Those conversions were done over many decades, under many different standards, and often without permits.

Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit buildings in Roanoke for investors who want them legal, safe and productive. We review the unit count, fire separation, egress, heating and shared utilities alongside unit finishes, and we phase work when tenants are in place. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, permits, Architectural Review Board approvals where needed, and inspections.

sections.body:
Old Southwest's large Victorian houses were built for single families, then divided into apartments as the neighborhood changed. Some conversions were done carefully, with proper separation and separate exits. Others left a single interior stair serving every unit, no fire-rated assemblies between floors, and shared electrical panels and boilers.

Before renovating, we confirm how many units the city recognizes and evaluate life safety. Typical corrective work includes fire-rated ceilings and walls between units, rated entry doors, interconnected smoke alarms and, where needed, a second means of egress. Adding exterior stairs or new openings in the H-2 district requires Architectural Review Board approval, which we plan into the schedule.

These buildings also carry the issues common to prewar Roanoke homes: stone foundations, old boilers and oil tanks, knob-and-tube wiring and lead paint. We price life-safety corrections alongside those items, so you have a realistic budget before purchase. Done right, an Old Southwest conversion can provide steady rents in a neighborhood close to downtown and the hospital.

sections.h2: Heating and utilities in Roanoke multi-unit buildings
sections.body:
Heating is often the most complicated system in a Roanoke small multifamily. Many converted buildings still run on a single boiler serving every unit, sometimes oil-fired, with the owner paying for heat. That arrangement increases operating cost and makes it harder to control individual unit temperatures.

We evaluate options for each building. Some boilers are in good condition and can be kept with zone controls. Others are near the end of life, and replacing them with individual heat pumps or ductless units for each apartment shifts heating costs to tenants and adds cooling. Oil tanks, whether in the basement or buried, are removed or properly abandoned.

Separating electric service is usually practical with new meters and panels. Separating water depends on the plumbing layout and is not always cost-effective. We price each option, so you can weigh upfront cost against long-term savings on utilities and maintenance. The goal is a building with predictable operating costs that fit the rents the neighborhood supports.

sections.h2: Phasing work in occupied Roanoke buildings
sections.body:
Many small multifamily buildings in Roanoke are purchased with tenants in place. Renovating without losing income requires a clear plan.

We begin with shared systems that affect the whole building: the roof, foundation drainage, main electrical service, heating plant and sewer line. Those items are scheduled with advance notice through your property manager and, for heating work, completed outside the coldest months when possible, so tenants are not left without heat.

Unit interiors are renovated as leases end, which keeps occupied units producing rent. Each unit has its own draw milestones and inspections, and your field manager coordinates access with tenants and the city's Planning, Building and Development department.

Exterior work in Old Southwest is sequenced around Architectural Review Board approval, so interior work continues while the exterior plan is reviewed. Masonry and concrete repairs are scheduled for warmer months, when mortar cures properly. That approach keeps the building safe, compliant and producing income throughout the renovation.

faqs.q: How do you confirm the legal unit count in a Roanoke building?
faqs.a: We review city records and compare them with the building's physical layout during the pre-offer review. Older Roanoke conversions sometimes have more apartments than the city recognizes, or units that do not meet current life-safety requirements. Confirming the legal count before purchase protects you from overpaying and helps plan any needed corrections. Third-floor and basement apartments in Old Southwest Victorians are the ones most often in question.

faqs.q: Should I replace a central boiler in a Roanoke multi-unit building?
faqs.a: Not always. A boiler in good condition with zone controls can work well. If it is near the end of its life or oil-fired, replacing it with individual heat pumps or ductless units can shift heating costs to tenants and add cooling. We lay both paths side by side, with the owner-paid heating cost of the boiler set against the installation cost of separate systems. Roanoke's colder winters make that owner-paid heat a bigger line item than it would be in Norfolk.

faqs.q: Does Old Southwest design review affect multifamily renovations?
faqs.a: Yes. Exterior changes visible from the street in the H-2 district, such as adding stairs, doors, windows or changing siding, require Architectural Review Board approval. Applications go in early, and interior work runs in parallel so the project does not stall while the exterior plan is reviewed. Fire escapes and exterior egress stairs are the items most likely to need discussion with the board, so we design them to sit at the rear of the house where possible.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Roanoke, VA | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Roanoke: Standard and Limited bids for bungalows, Victorians and postwar homes, with consultants, oil tanks and draws.
fha-203k.intro:
Roanoke has a large supply of older homes that suit renovation financing. Buyers can find Craftsman bungalows in Raleigh Court, frame homes in Belmont and postwar ranches along Williamson Road at prices that leave room for meaningful updates. An FHA 203(k) loan lets them finance the purchase and the renovation in a single mortgage, turning a house that needs a kitchen, heating system or foundation repair into a realistic option.

Genstone Construction, an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, works with Roanoke buyers, agents and lenders to prepare program-compliant bids, coordinate with HUD consultants on Standard loans, and complete work through the lender's draw process. Our bids reflect the issues common to Roanoke homes, including stone foundations, old heating systems, oil tanks and lead paint.

sections.h2: Choosing Standard or Limited for a Roanoke home
sections.body:
Non-structural work up to $75,000 can go through the Limited 203(k), which fits many Roanoke homes that need kitchen and bath updates, a new heating system, roof replacement, windows or flooring. Postwar ranches along Williamson Road and in Villa Heights are often good Limited candidates.

The Standard 203(k) is required when structural work is involved, such as repairing a bowing stone foundation wall, replacing rotted framing or reinforcing a sagging addition. That program carries a $5,000 minimum in eligible repairs and brings in a HUD-approved consultant to write up the work and sign off on each draw. Older homes in Belmont, Southeast and Old Southwest frequently need Standard loans because of foundation and framing issues.

We help buyers and agents choose correctly by inspecting the foundation, basement and framing during our walkthrough. A Roanoke bungalow may look cosmetic upstairs but have a stone foundation wall that needs structural repair. Identifying that early prevents a mid-process program change that delays closing and the start of work.

sections.h2: Roanoke conditions FHA will require corrected
sections.body:
FHA's minimum property standards require certain conditions to be corrected as part of a 203(k) loan. In Roanoke, the most common include deteriorated lead paint on pre-1978 homes, unsafe wiring such as knob-and-tube, inoperable or unsafe heating systems, missing handrails on stairs and porches, and water intrusion that threatens the structure.

Old oil tanks deserve special attention. Lenders and appraisers may flag a tank in the basement or evidence of a buried tank in the yard, and resolving it may involve testing, removal or proper abandonment. We look for tank evidence during our walkthrough and include the work in the bid.

Basement water intrusion on sloped lots is another common issue. Correcting drainage, repointing or parging foundations and adding gutters may be needed for the property to meet standards. Including those items in the initial bid helps avoid surprises during the appraisal or the final inspection, and ensures the buyer moves into a house that is safe, dry and functional.

sections.h2: Draws, consultants and timing in Roanoke
sections.body:
With a Standard loan in Roanoke, the consultant's write-up comes first and our pricing mirrors it item for item. With a Limited loan, our bid serves as the scope itself. Both include specific materials, quantities and labor, which lenders need for underwriting and appraisers need to estimate the after-improved value.

The lender keeps the renovation money in escrow after closing and pays it out only as inspected work is finished. Because Genstone never asks for money up front and bills each draw against completed milestones, that structure fits how we already run jobs.

Timing in Roanoke depends on season and location. Masonry and foundation work is best done in warmer months, and heating systems should be operational before winter if the buyer plans to move in. In Old Southwest, exterior changes require Architectural Review Board approval, which adds time. Our field manager handles permits with the city, schedules inspections and keeps the buyer and agent updated with photos and milestones throughout the project.

faqs.q: Which Roanoke homes fit a Limited 203(k)?
faqs.a: Postwar ranches and Cape Cods along Williamson Road, Villa Heights and Garden City often fit the Limited program because their structure is generally sound and their needs are kitchens, baths, heating, roofs and windows. Older homes with foundation or framing problems usually need the Standard program. We confirm which applies during our walkthrough, including a look at the basement walls on the downhill and uphill sides.

faqs.q: Will an oil tank affect my Roanoke 203(k)?
faqs.a: It might. Lenders and appraisers may require a tank to be tested, removed or properly abandoned. We look for tank evidence during our walkthrough and include the work in the bid, so it can be financed as part of the renovation rather than delaying the loan or becoming an unexpected cost. Asking the seller about past heating fuel early in the process can save time.

faqs.q: Can I do a 203(k) in Old Southwest?
faqs.a: Yes, but plan for Architectural Review Board approval on exterior changes and expect larger renovation scopes, since many Old Southwest homes need foundation, heating, wiring and exterior work. The Standard program is usually required. We help buyers and agents plan the timeline and budget accordingly. Buyers should also expect the contingency reserve to matter more on a Victorian, since concealed conditions behind plaster are common.

reo-renovation.title: REO and Bank-Owned Renovation in Roanoke, VA | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Roanoke REO renovations for banks, servicers and GSEs: frozen boilers, wet basements, oil tanks, code violations and complete draw documentation.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Roanoke
reo-renovation.intro:
A vacant house in Roanoke faces winter in a way vacant houses on the coast rarely do. Older homes with boilers and radiators can freeze and split if heat is lost, basements on sloped lots take on water during heavy rain, and stone foundations deteriorate when no one maintains the gutters. Add theft of copper and appliances and the code complaints that follow neglected properties, and an REO can lose value quickly.

Genstone Construction works with banks, mortgage servicers, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises to restore Roanoke REO properties to marketable condition. We are a preferred contractor for GSEs, and our process is built around documentation: photo-backed scopes, line-item estimates, permits, inspections and lien waivers. Genstone Field Services handles securing, preservation, winterization and inspections before renovation begins.

sections.h2: Freeze and water damage in vacant Roanoke homes
sections.body:
Roanoke winters are cold enough to cause serious freeze damage in vacant homes. Older houses with hydronic heating are especially vulnerable: if the boiler shuts down, water in radiators and pipes can freeze and split, flooding the house when temperatures rise. Even houses with forced-air systems can suffer split pipes in exterior walls and crawlspaces.

Water from the outside causes its own damage. Clogged gutters dump rain against foundations, and basements on sloped lots take on water through stone or brick walls. Over time, that leads to mold, rotted framing and damaged mechanicals.

We document conditions in detail during the initial inspection, with photos tied to each scope item. That includes testing heating systems for freeze damage, inspecting basements for water intrusion and checking framing for rot. The scope then addresses repairs in order of urgency, starting with stopping water intrusion and securing the property, so damage does not continue while the disposition decision is made.

Disposition decisions in Roanoke depend on the neighborhood and the property's condition. A Raleigh Court bungalow might justify a careful renovation, since renovated comparables sell well. A Southeast frame house might be better suited to safety and code repairs before sale to an investor.

We write scopes in tiers where that helps: a baseline safety and code package, a marketable-condition package and, where comparables support it, a fuller renovation. Each tier includes labor, materials and a draw schedule. Dumpster and debris costs are included in the estimate, which matters on properties with years of abandoned belongings.

Old oil tanks are flagged and priced, since they can complicate a sale. Where the buyer pool is likely to include FHA financing, we also flag conditions that would block an FHA appraisal, such as deteriorated lead paint, unsafe wiring, inoperable heating or missing handrails. That information helps the asset manager choose the right level of repair before listing.

sections.h2: Code compliance and documentation for Roanoke REO
sections.body:
Roanoke properties that sit vacant for long periods often accumulate code violations for overgrown yards, damaged porches, unsecured openings or deteriorated exteriors. We review any open violations, include corrections in the scope and coordinate with city inspectors to close them out.

Permits for electrical, plumbing, mechanical, roofing and structural work go through the city's Planning, Building and Development department. In the Old Southwest H-2 district, exterior changes need Architectural Review Board approval, which we plan for. Every trade on a Roanoke REO carries a Virginia Board for Contractors license and the insurance your guidelines call for, and each one signs a lien waiver before its draw is released.

Our field manager provides progress reports with photos and milestone updates, so servicers and GSE vendors can verify work remotely and release draws without sending inspectors to every stage. At completion, the asset manager receives a complete record of repairs, permits and inspections, which supports marketing and helps buyers and their lenders move through due diligence with confidence.

faqs.q: How do you handle freeze-damaged REO homes in Roanoke?
faqs.a: We inspect heating systems, radiators and plumbing for freeze damage, document conditions with photos and scope repairs. Older homes with boilers are particularly vulnerable. We also address water damage from split pipes, including mold remediation and replacement of damaged materials, so the property is safe and marketable. Cast-iron radiators that cracked in a freeze sometimes look intact, so each one is pressure-tested before the heat is restored.

faqs.q: Will an oil tank affect an REO sale in Roanoke?
faqs.a: It can. Buyers, lenders and insurers often ask about oil tanks. We look for evidence during the initial inspection and include testing, removal or proper abandonment in the scope, so the asset manager can resolve the issue before listing rather than during negotiations. Closure paperwork from the tank work is added to the property file for the listing agent and buyer.

faqs.q: Do you winterize vacant Roanoke properties?
faqs.a: Genstone Field Services handles winterization, securing, debris removal and inspections. In Roanoke, winterization is especially important for homes with boilers and radiators, which can freeze and split if heat is lost. Proper winterization protects the property while the asset manager decides on a disposition strategy. Hydronic systems need to be drained or filled with antifreeze, not just shut off, and the work is tagged so the next contractor knows what was done.
